what: Does the BLOCK_M=64 crossover move with KV depth on CUDA the way it does on gfx1100? Measured 2026-08-31 on one A100-SXM4-80GB at vllm#52684's author's request. It moves the other way.
why: Our earlier pass (../52684-blockm) fixes kv_len = q_len on all 140 rows and cannot speak to this axis. The author said so in the thread and asked for the run: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52684#issuecomment-5473180002
arms: his, so the two sets land on one axis: production = BLOCK_M 16 with Triton's default warp count, bm64 = BLOCK_M 64 with num_warps=4. speedup = production_ms / bm64_ms, so >1 means BLOCK_M=64 is faster.
forced_past_the_gate: Both arms, deliberately. The PR's gate is `q_len >= 512`, and the crossover under test sits at q_len 32-128, entirely below it; ../52684-blockm collapses every arm onto base there. The author forced the same way, through a launch proxy.
answer: On gfx1100 fixing kv_len at 4096 moves the crossover LEFT, from q_len 96-128 to 32-64. On the A100 the same fixed depth pushes the short-q region DOWN to 0.54-0.66, i.e. BLOCK_M=64 is 1.5-1.9x slower there. Same direction at 16384.

timing.pass1: one call between one pair of CUDA events
timing.pass2: 50 calls between one pair, divided -- run because pass 1's short-q rows sat near a constant ~0.2 ms and that had to be shown to be a real per-call cost rather than a measurement artefact
timing.verdict: the two agree to 0.88% at worst on four overlapping cells, so the constant is a per-call cost both arms pay -- the wrapper around the kernel -- and not a floor of the instrument
timing.dilution: because both arms pay it, the ratio is pulled toward 1 at small shapes; the kernel-level difference is larger than the ratio shows, in the same direction. The raw production_ms and bm64_ms columns are in the rows so this can be checked.

not_established: bf16 and head_size 128 only, two head patterns, one board, single-sequence prefill. No model-level TTFT claim. kv_len = q_len at q_len below 1024 is dominated by the per-call cost on both arms and is a control rather than a measurement.
